# Lattice-free container volume: exact variations and obstructions

This note examines a possible strengthening of the finite facet certificate
in `candidate 207a0b33a5d3a235`. It distinguishes (i) a maximum
of container volume, (ii) inclusion or fixed-direction maximality, and
(iii) first-order stationarity. These are different properties.

The unrestricted volume objective is unbounded even for a fixed actual,
full-dimensional, nonempty depth region avoiding the mixed lattice. A
conditional local-maximality hypothesis gives additional geometric contact
equations, proved below, but these equations alone do not repair the
previously falsified basin cap-budget inequality.

## 1. An actual full-dimensional depth region with unbounded container volume

Take `n=2,d=1` and

    C=[0,1]^2 x [-1,1],
    S={0,1}^2 x [-1,1],
    mu=H_1|S / 8,   alpha=1/5.

Thus `mu` is the normalized sum of the lengths of four fibers. Let

    D_alpha={w: every closed ambient halfspace containing w has mass>=alpha}.

The closed-halfspace representation in the cited facet note proves that
`D_alpha` is compact and convex and is contained in `C`.

Every point of `S` has depth at most `1/8`. Indeed, on its own interval
fiber choose a containing half-interval of length at most `1`. A sufficiently
large integer-coordinate tilt excludes the other three fibers while leaving
that restriction unchanged. More explicitly, at a binary vertex `v`, put
`q_v(z)=sum_j[(1-v_j)z_j+v_j(1-z_j)]`. This globally affine function equals
`|z_1-v_1|+|z_2-v_2|` on `[0,1]^2`; it is zero at `v` and at least one
at every other binary vertex. For an
own-fiber point `x_0`, choose `sigma in {-1,1}` with `sigma x_0>=0`.
The cap

    sigma x - 3q_v(z) >= sigma x_0

has the asserted own restriction and excludes the other fibers. Consequently
`D_alpha` contains no mixed-integer point.

The four points whose base indices are edge midpoints of the unit square
and whose continuous coordinate is zero have depth exactly `1/4`. For
example at `(0,1/2,0)`, the measure in the layer `z_1=0` is centrally
symmetric about the point and has total mass `1/2`. Every containing
closed halfspace therefore captures at least `1/4` from that layer.
Conversely a continuous halfspace through the point cuts this layer in
half, and an integer tilt excludes the other layer. The same argument
applies to all four edges. Hence the projection of `D_alpha` contains the
two-dimensional diamond with vertices the four edge midpoints.

The depth region itself is full dimensional in `R^3`. The ordinary center
`g=(1/2,1/2,0)` has depth at least `1/2` by central symmetry. Moving the
continuous coordinate by `h` changes the mass of a cap through this point
by at most `|h|/2`: for a nonvertical cap its cutoff in each of the four
unit-density interval fibers changes by `h`, giving total normalized loss
at most `4|h|/8`; a vertical cap is unchanged. Thus
`(1/2,1/2,1/4)` and `(1/2,1/2,-1/4)` both have depth at least `3/8`.
Together with the four edge-midpoint points, their convex hull is a
full-dimensional subset of `D_alpha`.

There is an explicit rational outer polygon for `K=pi(D_alpha)`. For every
binary vertex `v`,

    q_v(z)>=3/10  for every z in K.                  (1)

To prove this, suppose a candidate `(z_0,x_0) in C` has
`q=q_v(z_0)<3/10`. Choose `sigma x_0>=0` as before and use the cap

    sigma x - 2q_v(z) >= sigma x_0 - 2q.

At every other integer fiber its left side is at most `-1`, while the
right side is greater than `-3/5`; hence all those fibers are excluded.
At the vertex `v`, its interval length is at most `1+2q`. Its total mass
is at most `(1+2q)/8<1/5`. This proves (1), for arbitrary closed ambient
caps, without assuming fiber-parallel cuts.

Let the rational octagon be

    P_0={z in [0,1]^2:
          3/10<=z_1+z_2<=17/10,
          -7/10<=z_1-z_2<=7/10}.

Then `K subset P_0`. For `R>=1`, define the bounded polytope

    P_R=conv(P_0 union {(1/2,-R),(1/2,R)}).

Every point of `P_R` has first coordinate in `[0,1]`. Its sections at
first coordinate `0` and `1` remain exactly `[3/10,7/10]`: a convex
combination attaining an extreme first coordinate cannot use any of the
added points, whose first coordinate is `1/2`. Thus `P_R` contains NO
integer point, including on its boundary.

It contains `K`. Its area is at least `R`, because it contains the
quadrilateral with vertices

    (0,1/2), (1/2,-R), (1,1/2), (1/2,R),

whose area is exactly `R`. Therefore

    sup{area(L): L bounded convex, K subset L,
                     L intersect Z^2=empty}=infinity.              (2)

The same is true if only `int(L) intersect Z^2=empty` is required. Full
ambient bounded containers `P_R x [-2,2]` likewise contain `D_alpha`,
avoid `Z^2 x R`, and have volume tending to infinity.

This is a counterexample to automatic finite-volume attainment, even
when `D_alpha` is full dimensional. It is not an OC counterexample:
`alpha=1/5` exceeds the actual maximum mixed depth `1/8` of this body.

The distinction between closed exclusion and interior exclusion also
matters in one integer dimension. For a compact subset of `(0,1)`, closed
integer-free interval containers have length supremum `1`, which is not
attained. Interior-integer-free containers allow the interval `[0,1]`.

## 2. Lattice-preserving affine changes do not supply a base variation

An invertible affine map preserving `Z^n x R^d` bijectively has the form

    (z,x) -> (U z+k, A x+B z+b),
    U in GL_n(Z), k in Z^n, A in GL_d(R).             (3)

For completeness, a nonzero block from `x` into the first coordinate
would map a connected line to a nonconstant line inside `Z^n`, which is
impossible. The first-coordinate affine map therefore maps `Z^n`
bijectively onto itself, giving precisely the stated `U,k`; invertibility
then gives invertibility of `A`. The converse is immediate.

In a continuous family through the identity, `U` and `k` are locally
constant because their entries are integers. Thus every such genuinely
lattice-preserving variation fixes the integer projection pointwise.
It cannot change the projected container volume. Continuous fiber shears
or dilations can change fiber coordinates, but not this projection
objective.

The variations below are instead PHYSICAL deformations of the container
with the original lattice fixed. They are admissible only after checking
that lattice points do not enter. They are not coordinate normalizations
of `C`, `mu`, or the mixed lattice.

## 3. A conditional local-maximality theorem

Let `K` be a compact set strictly inside a bounded full-dimensional
polytope

    L={z:a_i.z<=b_i, i=1,...,r},   |a_i|=1,

whose facets `F_i` are nonredundant. Suppose `int(L) intersect Z^n` is
empty. Let `A_i=H_(n-1)(F_i)>0`, and let `c_i` be the facet centroid.
In dimension one, `A_i=1` and `c_i` is the endpoint, as usual.

Assume that `L` is a LOCAL maximum of ordinary `n`-dimensional volume
among bounded polyhedral containers of `K` which remain interior
lattice-free, allowing small independent changes of its facet normals
and offsets. No exterior bounding box or other shape restriction is
included in this hypothesis.

Then every facet has relative-interior lattice points, and

    c_i in conv(F_i relative interior intersect Z^n).              (4)

Equivalently there are nonnegative weights on the finite lattice set
`P_i=relint(F_i) intersect Z^n` satisfying

    sum_(p in P_i) lambda_ip=A_i,
    sum_(p in P_i) lambda_ip p=A_i c_i.             (5)

### Proof of the first-variation and feasibility statements

For small facet perturbations `(a_i,b_i)+t(delta a_i,delta b_i)`, the
volume derivative is

    delta |L| = sum_i A_i(delta b_i-c_i.delta a_i).                 (6)

Indeed the normal boundary speed at `z in F_i` is
`delta b_i-delta a_i.z`, because the original normal has unit length.
Integrating the resulting thin prism over the relative interior of each
facet gives (6). The overlaps or omissions near finitely many facet
edges have volume `O(t^2)`; deleting edge neighborhoods and then restoring
them gives the same formula for nonsimple polytopes. In dimension one
it is simply the difference of the two endpoint velocities.

Fix one facet `i` and vary only its inequality. All lattice points on
other facets remain outside the new interior. In particular a lattice
point on an edge of `F_i` remains excluded by an unchanged facet. The
only boundary lattice points requiring a constraint are `p in P_i`,
and their exact sufficient constraints are

    delta b_i-delta a_i.p<=0.                       (7)

These are linear, not merely tangent approximations: substituting a
fixed contact point in the perturbed inequality gives precisely `t`
times (7). All initially exterior lattice points remain exterior for
sufficiently small `t`. To see this uniformly, the perturbed polytopes
lie in one fixed ball: positive spanning of the original normals is
stable under small perturbations. There are only finitely many lattice
points in that ball, and every initially exterior one has a strictly
violated inequality. The compact set `K` remains inside by its positive
distance from every original facet.

Thus every vector satisfying (7) is an actual feasible one-sided
variation. Local maximality and (6) imply

    A_i(delta b_i-c_i.delta a_i)<=0

on this finite polyhedral cone. Finite-dimensional Farkas separation
therefore expresses its linear functional as a nonnegative combination
of the functionals in (7):

    A_i(delta b_i-c_i.delta a_i)
      =sum_(p in P_i) lambda_ip(delta b_i-p.delta a_i).

Comparing the offset and normal coefficients gives (5). If `P_i` were
empty, an outward offset increase would be feasible and would increase
volume, a contradiction. This completes the proof.

### Exact global equations and homotheties

The facet divergence identities are

    sum_i A_i a_i=0,
    sum_i A_i a_i c_i^T=|L| I_n.

They follow by integrating, respectively, a constant vector field and
the coordinate-linear vector fields over the boundary. Substitution of
(5) yields the explicit lattice-contact stress

    sum_(i,p) lambda_ip a_i=0,
    sum_(i,p) lambda_ip a_i p^T=|L| I_n.             (8)

Taking the trace gives the exact scalar coefficient

    sum_(i,p) lambda_ip a_i.p=n |L|.                (9)

These equations involve ordinary container volume. They do not replace
the original mixed-integer measure by an integral over the projection.

For an affine physical deformation `z -> z+t(Bz+q)`, the volume derivative
is `|L| tr(B)`. At a facet lattice contact `p`, the outward normal velocity
is `a_i.(Bp+q)`. At every boundary lattice point, select one facet
containing it, including at points on several facets. If every selected
velocity is strictly negative, the deformation is feasible for small
positive `t`. This requires control of all boundary lattice points, not
only those with positive weights in (8). Nonpositive selected velocities
can be handled for a first-order necessary condition by adding an
arbitrarily small inward homothety about a fixed interior point.
Equation (8) consequently gives

    |L| tr(B)=sum_(i,p) lambda_ip a_i.(Bp+q)<=0

for these feasible first-order affine directions. An outward homothety
has derivative `n|L|>0`, but is INADMISSIBLE: every relative-interior
lattice contact enters the interior. Hence outward scaling cannot be
inserted into a cap inequality as if it were a free test direction.

## 4. Exact distinction between stationarity and maximality

Consider the lattice-free diamond

    L_0={|z_1-1/2|+|z_2-1/2|<=1}.

Its four facet centroids are exactly the four binary lattice points.
Each facet has length `sqrt(2)`. Thus (5)--(9) hold, with the entire
facet weight on its single binary contact. Its area is `2`.

With these four normal directions held fixed, `L_0` is an attained
strict local volume maximum among interior-lattice-free offset changes.
Every binary contact strictly satisfies the other three facet inequalities.
An outward change of its own facet offset therefore places that lattice
point in the interior for all sufficiently small changes of the other
offsets. Every feasible sufficiently small offset change is consequently
coordinatewise inward, unless it is zero.

But free facet directions admit the exact family

    L_s={(1+s)|z_1-1/2|+(1-s)|z_2-1/2|<=1},  |s|<1.

It is interior lattice-free: for every integer point, both absolute
coordinate differences are at least `1/2`, so the displayed left side
is at least `1`. It contains the entire unit square, and therefore the
depth-region projection from Section 1. That projection is strictly
inside each `L_s`, since it lies in `P_0`, which omits the four corners.
Its exact area is

    |L_s|=2/(1-s^2).

Thus its first derivative at zero is zero, but its second derivative is
`4>0`. The full first-order lattice-contact equations do not make `L_0`
a free-shape local maximum, and free-shape stationarity alone does not
establish maximality or compactness.

There is also an exact cap-budget audit of these extra first-order
equations. The expanded witness container in
`candidate d0f838592db846be` is precisely `L_0`, written
as `0<=z_1+z_2<=2` and `|z_1-z_2|<=1`. Thus that already-audited example
satisfies all equations (5)--(9), as well as fixed-normal local volume
maximality, all positive cap circuits, and all attained real contacts.
Nevertheless its proposed basin promotion fails by exactly

    gamma_2 M_basin - max_j mu(H_j)=91/7500>0.

The old obstruction therefore survives the new first-order container
conditions. It does not satisfy a below-OC budget and does not possess
the stronger, free-shape local maximum hypothesis.

## 5. Artificial bounds and the original cap certificate

Adding an exterior bounding set can restore finite-volume attainment,
but its contact constraints must then appear in the variation equations.
For a concrete illustration, restrict containers to lie in the octagon
`P_0` of Section 1. The unique maximum-volume container of `K` in that
class is `P_0` itself: it is feasible, and any proper closed convex subset
has smaller area. Yet `P_0` has no integer point even on its boundary.
Its stationarity is supplied entirely by the artificial outer constraint,
not by lattice contacts. Equations (4)--(9) cannot be asserted in this
bounded class while omitting those outer forces.

There is a separate loss in moving freely from the original auxiliary
projection to a new container. The original finite facet certificate
assigns at most `d+1` cap inequalities to a projection FACET because its
normal is a single minimal positive continuous-normal circuit. An arbitrary
supporting direction can require several such circuits. For example take
`n=3,d=1`, `0<r<1/6`, and the nonvertical auxiliary system

    epsilon_i(z_i-1/2)+eta x<=r
    for i=1,2,3 and epsilon_i,eta in {-1,1}.

Its projection is exactly `[1/2-r,1/2+r]^3`, by taking `x=0`. The
globally maximal interior-lattice-free split

    1<=z_1+z_2+z_3<=2

contains this projection strictly. Its facet normal `(1,1,1)` cannot be
represented using only `d+1=2` original inequalities: every original
integer normal has only one nonzero coordinate, so the sum of two cannot
have three nonzero coordinates. An actual Farkas representation exists
using more inequalities, but the one-circuit cardinality is lost.

For completeness, this split is maximal by inclusion. In coordinates
with first coordinate `z_1+z_2+z_3`, obtained by an integer unimodular
map, it is `[1,2] x R^2`. The map can be taken to have rows
`(1,1,1),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)`, with determinant one. Suppose an enlarged convex
set also contains `p=(p_1,p')` with `p_1<1`. Choose `t in (0,1)` such that
`1=t p_1+(1-t)(3/2)`, and put
`q=(3/2,-t p'/(1-t))`. Then `q` is in the interior of the split and
`(1,0,0)=t p+(1-t)q`. A small ball around `q` lies in the split, so its
image under this affine combination is a ball around the lattice point
`(1,0,0)` inside the enlarged convex set. This contradicts lattice
freeness. If `p_1>2`, the same construction produces the interior lattice
point `(2,0,0)`. Thus no strict convex enlargement is lattice-free. This
proves maximality without assuming that a new facet is an old projection
facet.

## Conclusion and scope

The valid additional information is the conditional facet-centroid and
matrix stress (5)--(9), with coefficient `n` in the homothetic trace.
Automatic finite-volume attainment is false, and first-order container
stationarity is compatible with an existing exact cap-promotion failure.
No sharp mixed-volume budget has been inferred from these equations.
